analysis.body:
# AI in Sports

According to the Census Bureau, 20.0% of firms in arts, entertainment, and recreation—the category that includes sports—reported using AI in the two weeks before the survey, up from 16.6% in the prior period. This measured adoption reflects growing AI use across the industry, though the census data do not isolate sports from the broader arts and entertainment sector, making it difficult to assess adoption specific to sports organizations alone.

The dominant application of AI in sports is video analysis and performance tracking. Hudl, which sets the standard for video analysis across high school, college, and professional programs, deploys AI-powered Focus cameras for automated game capture and uses computer-vision technology to assist scouting and player development. Catapult and Kinexon provide wearable and tracking platforms that apply AI to athlete monitoring, biomechanics analysis, and load management—tools used across NCAA and professional leagues. These platforms represent the primary vectors through which AI reaches coaching staffs and training facilities.

Governance bodies shape the deployment landscape. The NCAA governs technology policy across more than 1,000 member schools in three divisions, and decisions about recruiting analytics, roster management, and transfer-portal use influence how AI tools are adopted at the college level. The National Federation of State High School Associations monitors scholastic sports technology for 12,000 member schools, affecting deployment in secondary sports. The Sports and Fitness Industry Association publishes research on technology adoption in youth and scholastic sports, tracking both participation trends and equipment markets, though the sourced excerpts do not detail specific findings on AI ROI or risk assessments.

The Sports Tech Research Network, a nonprofit founded from Ghent University's innovation consortium, bridges academic research with commercial development of sports technologies. STRN emphasizes trustworthy and science-based solutions through multi-disciplinary collaboration between academia, industry, and field practitioners, and has published frameworks for quality assessment of sports technology. This institutional focus on evidence-based deployment suggests the industry recognizes that effective AI adoption requires validation beyond vendor claims.

The sources do not provide specific revenue figures for AI vendors in sports, detailed ROI evidence from deployed systems, or documentation of regulatory restrictions on AI use beyond governance oversight of recruiting and transfer rules. For organizations considering AI deployment, the evidence indicates that video analysis and athlete monitoring are proven use cases with established vendors and industry adoption, but decision-makers should defer to their governing body's policies on recruiting and roster analytics, and may benefit from engagement with research-backed validation frameworks rather than vendor-led implementation alone.

https://sfia.org/.brief: SFIA released a 2026 report examining participation across 30 sports, analyzing why people engage in team sports and how costs affect participation rates. The organization also published 92 single-sport reports providing five-year participation trends broken down by demographic factors including gender, age, education, geography, income, and ethnicity, plus cross-participation data with other activities. These reports are positioned as early indicators to help industry leaders plan for 2025 trends.
